Context' contains '### 1.1 Prior situation' (the single cron process in a long-lived pod, with a before-state Mermaid diagram and four structural problems), '### 1.2 Motivation for the change' (react to something happening rather than the next poll, isolate the channels, make cost track volume, deploy and scale each channel independently), and '### 1.4 Scope' (in scope: the transport and dispatch path; out of scope: content and templating, preferences and opt-outs, provider selection, in-app/websocket).

expectations.text: Claims about the prior situation are either sourced (file, dashboard, ticket, metric) or explicitly labelled as assumed
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs, read as universal per the eval instruction): every specific factual claim about the pre-migration system that the user did not supply and that does not follow from the described topology must carry a source or an explicit uncertainty label. Partly done - the polling mechanism is labelled ('it looked for work that was due (pending rows in the database `[A-1]`)') and A-1 is in the assumptions register. But the numbered list of the cron's four problems, which the document presents as fact ('That shape had four structural problems, and they are the reason the migration happened'), carries no labels. Violating instances: 'The pod was sized for the worst tick and paid for around the clock, including the hours with no notifications at all' (a claim about the old pod's sizing and cost profile that was never supplied and does not follow from 'a cron running in a pod'; the document itself later asks for the volume and cost numbers in Open questions 3 and 4) and 'an unhandled error anywhere could abort the run, including work already queued behind it in the same batch' (depends on the old code's error handling, which the document has no access to). Symmetry note: the with_skill run fails on the same class of claim ('One pod's cost, constant whether or not anything was sent'), so this verdict is identical for both.

expectations.text: Architecture section lists the components with their responsibilities (EventBridge, per-channel Lambdas, etc.)
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): a components list or set of component sections naming each part and what it is responsible for. Met: '## 3. Architecture' has a static Mermaid view plus one subsection per component - 3.2 the event and the bus ('A producer calls PutEvents on a custom event bus... The producer's responsibility ends there'), 3.3 rules one per notification type ('whose event pattern selects that channel's events and whose single target is that channel's function'), 3.4 one Lambda per channel ('owns dispatch end to end: validate the payload, resolve the recipient's address or device token, render the content, call the provider, interpret the provider's response, and record the outcome'), 3.5 dead-letter queues and the archive, 3.6 idempotency, 3.7 observability. Each subsection also names the requirements it serves.

expectations.text: Includes at least one step-by-step numbered flow of the event-driven process
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): at least one ordered, numbered walk-through of the runtime event path. Met: '### 3.8 Dynamic view - dispatch of one notification' gives a Mermaid sequence diagram followed by 'Step by step, in words - the numbered form is what to walk through with a newcomer', with 8 numbered steps from '1. A domain thing happens' and the PutEvents publish through '3. Rules evaluate the event', '5. The function claims the notificationId', to '8. On exhaustion the event lands in the channel's DLQ'. Section 6.4 adds a second numbered procedure for adding a notification type.

expectations.text: Has a risks-and-mitigations section
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): a dedicated section pairing risks with mitigations. Met: '## 5. Risks in the deployed architecture, and how they are managed' is a table with columns # | Risk | Impact | Prob. | Mitigation | Contingency and 9 rows R-1..R-9 (silent drop, duplicate notification, concurrency stampede against a provider rate limit, distributed debugging cost, DLQ as a silent data-loss buffer, cold start latency, fire-and-forget mistaken for delivery, envelope schema drift, payload growth). Every row has a populated impact, probability, mitigation and contingency.

expectations.text: Has a lessons-learned section containing at least one concrete lesson discovered by doing the work, not only a heading or generic advice
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs, and the point on which iteration 1's judges split): the section must contain at least one lesson that is both concrete and presented as learned by doing this work; a heading alone, generic advice, or lessons derived from documentation or from the architecture's structure do not satisfy it. The section exists and its lessons are concrete and migration-specific ('The failure mode changed shape, not just size. A cron fails loudly... An event bus fails quietly'; 'Guarantees the single process gave away for free became explicit work'), which clears the 'not only a heading or generic advice' half. But the section opens by disclaiming the other half: 'The lessons that follow are the ones this architecture *implies*, derived from its structure rather than collected from the team. Treat them as a starting draft: replace them with what actually went wrong during the migration... they cannot be inferred `[A-14]`.' A-14 in the register repeats it. reply.md repeats it again: 'Lessons learned is a draft I derived from the architecture, not from your team.' So nothing in the section is presented as discovered by doing the work. Symmetry note: with_skill fails on the same ground, its lessons being labelled [platform] and read from AWS documentation.

expectations.text: Defines the domain terms and acronyms it uses, in a glossary or inline at first use
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): the domain vocabulary the document leans on must be defined, by glossary or where the term is introduced; industry-standard abbreviations the stated audience (an engineer joining an AWS team) is expected to know - SQS, HTTP, TTL, FIFO, p95, K8s/ECS - need not be expanded. Met by the inline route rather than a glossary: 3.2 defines the event and the custom bus and shows the envelope as annotated JSON, naming the routing key and the idempotency key as the two fields with architectural weight; 3.3 defines rules and targets ('Rules are independent subscriptions to the same event, not a chain'); 3.5 defines and contrasts the target DLQ and the bus archive in a table of what each catches and does not catch; 3.6 defines idempotency as 'a first-writer-wins check on the event's notificationId before contacting the provider'; the RF-n / RNF-n ID scheme is anchored by the '2.1 Functional' and '2.2 Non-functional' headings it sits under. Below the bar, and the same latitude was given to with_skill: 'DLQ' is first used in the Related documents list before section 3.5 explains it, and 'ADR-style' and 'MSK' appear once each without expansion.

expectations.text: Includes a version-history table (version, date, author, description)
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): a table under a version-history heading carrying all four columns. Met: '## Version history' with header '| Version | Date | Author | Description |' and one row - '1.0 | 2026-09-08 | `<author>` | Document created from a verbal description of the migration; assumptions and open questions marked for team confirmation.' The Author cell is an explicit placeholder, which reply.md flags to the user ('the author field are placeholders').

expectations.text: Written entirely in English
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): no non-English prose anywhere, including headings, tables, Mermaid labels and figure captions. Met: verified by reading all 600 lines and by grepping for Portuguese function words and non-ASCII characters - the only non-ASCII hits are em dashes, arrows and the section sign. Diagram labels, the JSON envelope keys and the references are English.

expectations.text: Frames the document retrospectively (documents what was built) rather than proposing a choice between alternatives
expectations.evidence: STANDARD (applied to both runs): the frame must be a record of a shipped system; an alternatives comparison is permitted only if explicitly retrospective and not putting a choice to the reader. Met: the header states 'Type: retrospective technical documentation (ADR-style record of an implementation already in production)', 1.3 'What was built' ends 'This is live in production', and section 5 is titled 'Risks in the deployed architecture'. Section 4 is titled 'Alternatives considered', which is proposal-shaped on its face, but it is explicitly retrospective in its own opening - 'the migration is already shipped, and this table is reconstructed from the shape of the result, not transcribed from the decision meeting... If a written record of that discussion exists, it supersedes this table `[A-13]`' - the deployed option is marked '(chosen)', and the analysis justifies what exists rather than asking the reader to pick. reply.md states the same framing. Judged the same way as with_skill's comparison section, which carries an equivalent disclaimer.

expectations.text: Records Kafka, the company API standard, the coverage gate and AWS as constraints, prior decisions or givens in a section separate from the requirements
expectations.evidence: Three of the four are recorded outside the requirements, in '§3 What was asked, and how it is classified': Kafka as 'Constraint C1, not a requirement', AWS as 'Constraint C2', the coverage gate as 'Not architecturally relevant — an engineering standard, tracked in CI' (and §4 confirms 'Dropped from the drivers: 90% test coverage'). The API standard is not: the classification table records it as '| 2 | Endpoints follow the company API standard | **Requirement N5** (architecturally relevant) | A public contract is expensive to change ... Passes the *hard to reverse* test.' and §4 lists it among the non-functional requirements — 'N5 — Endpoints follow the company API standard (C2/item 2): resource naming, pagination shape, filter syntax, error envelope, auth.' So one of the four items the assertion names is recorded as a requirement, not as a constraint, prior decision or given.

expectations.text: Each of those items carries a source (who or what imposed or decided it)
expectations.evidence: Only Kafka is attributed: 'C1 — Kafka is the event transport. Decided by the platform team.' AWS is given its rationale but no decider ('C2 — Runs on AWS. Everything else runs there; a second cloud would add a network boundary...'), which I am reading as a provenance statement (the existing estate) and letting stand. The coverage gate carries no attribution at all — 'an engineering standard, tracked in CI' classifies the item without saying who set 90% or who could change it. The API standard likewise names no author or owning body; the nearest thing is the owner column of an open question, '| Q2 | Where is the company API standard ... | API governance |', which attributes the question rather than the standard. A reader cannot tell who to approach to challenge either item.

expectations.text: Each of those items carries an indication of the cost or difficulty of challenging or reversing it
expectations.evidence: Three of four are covered. Kafka: §7 gives the cost of the constraint on this problem and 'What would reopen it: if topic onboarding blocks Phase 2 for more than about two weeks, or if the platform team confirms that no second consumer is planned within a year ... it is worth asking them to reconsider — cheaply, because Phase 1 ships without the topic'. AWS: 'a second cloud would add a network boundary, a second security model, and a second on-call surface for no benefit'. API standard: 'A public contract is expensive to change once compliance and a future UI depend on it. Passes the *hard to reverse* test.' The coverage gate has none. The only adjacent text is 'It does not force a component, a boundary, or an integration to exist; the design is identical at 90% and at 70%', which speaks to the architecture's insensitivity to the number, not to what challenging or reversing the gate would cost; §9 only restates that it is 'enforced in CI'.

expectations.text: The 'nice to have' log-browsing UI does not appear as a requirement
expectations.evidence: Absent from F1-F5 and N1-N10. Recorded in §2 Out of scope: '**A browsing UI.** The user named it as a nice-to-have; it is deferred deliberately (§9, Phase 4)', classified in §3 as '**Non-goal for v1**, with a design obligation', and reappears only as launch Phase 4. §4 closes with 'Dropped from the drivers: ... and the browsing UI (§2, out of scope)'.

expectations.text: 'It should be fast' is either turned into a non-functional requirement with a quantified metric and target, or explicitly flagged as not yet a requirement because it has no metric
expectations.evidence: Both halves are done. §3: '"It should be fast" — **Not a requirement as stated** — replaced by N1, N2, N3, N4 ... "Fast" hides the decision instead of making it.' The replacements are quantified: 'N1 — Write-path overhead <= 10 ms p95', 'N2 — Freshness: an event is queryable within 60 s p95', 'N3 — Interactive query <= 2 s p95 ... Cold-window queries ... asynchronous, <= 15 min', 'N4 — Export: 1,000,000 rows in <= 15 min'. All four are labeled as assumption A4 ('these are *proposed* budgets for compliance to confirm, not measured or agreed ones').

expectations.text: Test coverage above 90% is not listed as a non-functional requirement of the running system
expectations.evidence: Not among N1-N10. §3 classifies it '**Not architecturally relevant** — an engineering standard, tracked in CI ... Kept as a delivery gate in §9, out of the drivers'; §4 states '**Dropped from the drivers:** 90% test coverage (an engineering standard, enforced in CI — §9)'; it recurs only as a §9 delivery gate.

expectations.text: At least one functional requirement is derived from the compliance-team pain described in the last sentence, with its goal stated and the compliance role named
expectations.evidence: F3 names the role and states the objective inside the requirement: '**F3 — Structured query by the compliance team.** They must be able to filter by actor, action type, entity type + entity id, and time range, in any combination, and page through the results — without engineering assistance and without writing SQL.' The derivation is explicit — §3 records the closing sentence as '**The requirement** (F1-F4, N1-N4) ... it is the only item that would still matter if all the others were withdrawn' — and §2 states the goal it serves: 'Every action taken in the admin panel must land in a durable, tamper-evident store that the compliance team can query themselves, without engineering in the loop.' F4 (bulk export 'so compliance can attach it to a case file or hand it to an external auditor') is derived the same way. The document has no goals table, so the goal is carried in the requirement sentence and the problem statement rather than in an explicit traced link; the assertion's words do not require the latter.

expectations.text: The document explicitly tells the reader which of the user's items were reclassified and why
expectations.evidence: §3 is exactly this: a six-row table with columns '# | As stated | Classified as | Why', introduced by 'The request arrived as six numbered items plus a closing sentence. The closing sentence is the actual requirement; several of the numbered items are not requirements at all. Sorting this out is the first piece of architectural work ... three of the six items would otherwise silently decide the design for us.' The reply points the reader at it first: 'Read §3 first — I reclassified most of what you sent'.

expectations.text: The tradeoff analysis evaluates at least one alternative to Kafka rather than treating the platform team's choice as the only option
expectations.evidence: Passes on substance, in §7 rather than in the §6 tables. §7 argues both sides and names the no-broker design as a live option: 'the delivery guarantee F1 needs is supplied by the outbox and the idempotent write, not by the broker. What Kafka adds is a schema contract, a DLQ, a consumer group, offset semantics, a partitioning-key decision, and a second team's onboarding process, for a stream assumed at roughly 6 events/second ... For a single-producer, single-consumer path, the simplest design that meets every requirement in §4 is outbox -> worker -> Aurora + S3, with no broker at all', followed by 'What would reopen it' with two named triggers. §6 also rejects the naive Kafka shape ('A2 — Produce to Kafka directly from the request path') on requirements. So Kafka is not treated as the only option. Caveat recorded under assertion 10: the non-Kafka option never enters the alternatives analysis, whose transport dimension is titled '### Dimension D — Kafka flavour (within C1)'.

expectations.text: Where an alternative conflicts with a stated given, the conflict is recorded as a cost rather than used to exclude the option before analysis
expectations.evidence: The given narrows the option set instead of being priced inside an option. The transport dimension of the alternatives analysis is scoped by the constraint on its face — '### Dimension D — Kafka flavour (within C1)' — and its three rows (D1 reuse the platform MSK cluster, D2 dedicated MSK Serverless, D3 self-operated provisioned MSK) are all Kafka, so the one option that conflicts with C1 gets no row and therefore no pros/cons/risk/impact/probability/mitigation/contingency treatment while every other option in §6 gets one. §7 opens from acceptance rather than from analysis — 'C1 is accepted, and this section exists so that acceptance is *informed* rather than silent' — and §8 records it as settled by ownership rather than by weighing: '**C1 (Kafka) belongs to the platform team and is taken as given**'. What §7 prices is the cost of honouring the constraint and of asking the platform team to revisit it; what it never does is carry the conflict as a cost attached to an evaluated alternative. (No option in §6 conflicts with C2/AWS, so AWS is untested by this assertion here.)

expectations.text: The p95 dashboard-endpoint figure is stated with its source (the Grafana 'api-latency' board) next to the claim
expectations.evidence: Source sits with the claim at first statement: "the dashboard endpoint's p95 was around 8 seconds last month** (`api-latency` Grafana board)". The provenance table repeats it as a row: "E1 | Dashboard endpoint p95 ≈ **8s** last month | `api-latency` Grafana board, as reported by the requester | **Reported, not verified.**" N1 ties the target back to the same instrument ("measured on the `api-latency` Grafana board so the before/after comparison uses the same instrument that produced E1"), and Q5 asks which panel produced it.

expectations.text: The location of the report queries is cited concretely (reports/queries.py)
expectations.evidence: Cited by path and treated as an unverified claim about a specific file: "These queries live in **`reports/queries.py`**"; "E3 | Report queries live in **`reports/queries.py`** | Reported by the requester | **Reported, file not inspected.**"; F2 "Every report currently in `reports/queries.py`"; Q3 "Is `reports/queries.py` the only place reporting queries live?"; task P0.1 attributes execution time to "the queries in `reports/queries.py`".

expectations.text: The 40% database-load figure, which the prompt states with no source, is not repeated as established fact: it carries a label (assumed, estimated, unverified, or 'per the requester') rather than being presented as measured
expectations.evidence: The label exists ("E2 | Reporting is **~40%** of database load | Reported by the requester; underlying source not named | **Reported, not verified, and the metric is undefined**"), but the figure is then repeated as established fact in the Context prose that carries the argument, which is what this assertion bars. Two violating instances, both unhedged declaratives: "the load share means reporting is not a rounding error we can tune away at the margins — it is a structural half of what the database does. Both numbers point the same direction: the two workloads need to stop sharing one instance." And, in the problem framing: "**Problem A — contention.** Reporting consumes ~40% of the database and thereby degrades *transactional* endpoints." Neither sentence carries assumed, reported, estimated or 'per the requester', and the second also asserts the causal link that the same document elsewhere labels an inference (E5). The blanket disclaimer "nothing here is independently verified" and the E2 row do not undo a restatement that presents the number as measured at the point where it drives the conclusion.

expectations.text: For the 40% figure, the document names what would confirm it (a specific query, tool, or measurement)
expectations.evidence: A named tool and a named analysis: task "P0.1 Load attribution | `pg_stat_statements` analysis; rank reporting queries by total execution time; define what \"40% of load\" actually measures (Q2) | 1–2d". Phase 0 restates it ("Enable/read `pg_stat_statements` and attribute execution time to the queries in `reports/queries.py`"), N3 lists "`pg_stat_statements` attribution (Phase 0)", and Q2 states what the measurement must settle ("CPU time, total statement execution time, and query count imply materially different situations, and N2's exit criterion has to be expressed in the same metric").

expectations.text: Quantitative claims in the context carry either a source or a label indicating how they are known
expectations.evidence: Every distinct quantitative claim in the Context section has provenance, and the section is explicit that none of it is first-hand: "Every number in this RFC comes from the request that prompted it. The author had no access to the Grafana board, the repository, or the database while writing, so nothing here is independently verified." The E1–E6 table gives each figure a source column and a status, and it also records what is absent ("E6 | Data volume, growth rate, per-tenant skew | — | **Absent.**") and separates inference from evidence ("E5 … **Inference, not evidence.**"). Invented targets are marked too: N1 "(assumed target)", N2 "≤ 10%" against "the reported ~40%", N5 "(assumed budget)", A5's 15 minutes as an assumption, and "Estimates are **unvalidated**". Judged per distinct claim, coverage is complete; note that individual restatements in prose are not always hedged (see assertion 3), and under a per-mention reading this assertion would fail on the same quotes.

expectations.text: At least one requirement traces explicitly back to a specific fact stated in the context
expectations.evidence: Requirements cite the evidence IDs directly. N1: "Dashboard endpoint p95 ≤ 1.5s and p99 ≤ 3s (assumed target), measured on the `api-latency` Grafana board** so the before/after comparison uses the same instrument that produced E1." N2: "reporting's share of primary database load must fall to ≤ 10%** (from the reported ~40%), measured by whatever metric turns out to underlie E2 once Q2 is answered." N3 justifies itself against E5 ("its absence is part of why E5 is currently an inference"), and F2 traces to the file named in the context.

expectations.text: The reasoning can be followed without opening any linked or external resource
expectations.evidence: No hyperlink exists in the document (the Related-documents entries read "*Link needed.*" and "*Not inspected for this draft.*"), and the argument does not defer to them: the two-problem framing, the E-table, the requirement list, the tradeoff tables and the phasing are all stated in the text. The sequence diagram is deliberately duplicated in prose — "**Step by step, in words** (so the flow survives without the diagram renderer)" — and the traceability table restates which component meets each requirement.

expectations.text: Provenance for the facts appears in the document (for example a sources section or inline citations) rather than only as a list of related documents at the top
expectations.evidence: The top-of-document "Related documents" list is not the only provenance: a dedicated "### Evidence and its provenance" subsection carries a six-row table with Claim / Source / Status per fact, and the facts are cited inline afterwards by ID (E1, E2, E3, E5, E6) in the requirements, the design, the decision and the open questions. The related-documents list itself also states status rather than merely linking ("Source of the \"reporting is 40% of database load\" figure — **unidentified**; needs naming").

notes: All figures are reported by the requester and unverified; E5 (that reporting contention causes the 8 s p95) is explicitly an inference
PostgreSQL, managed hosting, Python, and tenant scoping inside the queries are all assumptions (A1–A3, A7)
The 15-minute staleness budget (A5) is flagged as the assumption most likely to be wrong and most consequential
Data volume, growth rate and per-tenant skew are absent (E6/Q1), so the design states it cannot be sized quantitatively
Q4 (per-report staleness tolerance) is blocking for Phase 2 and is called a product decision, not the author's
Author field and the `api-latency` board URL are left as TBD placeholders to be filled before circulating
Roadmap estimates are marked unvalidated and to be redone after Phase 0
No system access, so the whole evidence base was recorded in an E1–E6 provenance table and a measurement-only Phase 0 was placed before any build work

expectations.text: The document states explicitly that the items the user listed are design choices rather than requirements
expectations.evidence: §1: "Alongside the problem, a set of solutions has been proposed: adopt the saga pattern, split checkout into microservices, add Redis caching, use gRPC between services, and introduce a feature flag system. These arrived framed as requirements. They are not requirements - they are candidate designs, and §2.1 handles that reclassification explicitly." §2.1's table classifies four as "Candidate solution" and the fifth as "Partly a real requirement", restating it as the reversibility requirement rather than the platform. §2.1 also states the reason: "The five items in the request describe *how*, not *what must be true*."

expectations.text: None of the saga pattern, microservices, Redis caching, gRPC or feature flags appears in the requirements section as a requirement
expectations.evidence: The enumerated requirements are R1-R5 (per-step attribution, failure taxonomy, no inconsistent terminal state, idempotent retry, retrospective diagnosis) and NFR1-NFR5 (no degradation, reversibility, time to attribute, no sensitive data in telemetry, bounded cost). None is a saga, a service split, Redis, gRPC or a flag platform. The five items appear in the section only in the §2.1 reclassification table, routed to §4. NFR2 mentions the flag system but states the requirement as the capability: "Every change introduced by this work is reversible in under 5 minutes without a code deploy. This is the real requirement behind 'feature flag system'." Noted against the assertion's wording: the §2.1 cell for the flag system reads "Partly a real requirement", the closest thing in either document to readmitting a listed item - but the requirement it implies is stated as reversibility, and §4.3/§5.1 evaluate the platform as one option among three and do not adopt it.

expectations.text: At least one requirement is derived from the 2% checkout failure rate, with a goal, and a target that is either derived from a stated fact or explicitly labelled as assumed
expectations.evidence: No requirement is traced to the failure rate. The 2% appears only in §1 Context, in §1.1 out of scope, in §4 risk cells, in §4.5's objection, in assumption A-1 and in the "Baseline measurement" task ("Reproduce the 2% figure; record its query, window, and denominator") - never in §2. §2 derives R1-R5 and NFR1-NFR5 from the diagnosability half of the problem only; §1 says so outright: "That number on its own is not the problem this RFC exists to solve." No requirement bounds, baselines or targets the failure rate (no guardrail that it must not rise, no reduction goal), and §2.4 confirms the omission was deliberate: "no latency target for checkout itself (none was given), no throughput or scaling ceiling". The nearest candidates fail the assertion's other halves too: NFR1's "≤ 20ms and ≤ 5% of current checkout p95" is derived from instrumentation overhead rather than the 2%, and its 20 ms is neither derived from a stated fact nor labelled as assumed (current p95 is unknown - it is open question 6). R2's "under 5% of failures" target bounds the unclassified bucket, i.e. the diagnosability gap, not the rate. Requirements also carry no goal field.

expectations.text: At least one requirement is derived from the inability to identify which checkout step failed, expressed measurably
expectations.evidence: R1: "For every checkout attempt, the system records which steps were entered, which completed, and which one failed, under a single identifier... Verifiable: given any failed attempt ID from the last 30 days, an engineer can name the failing step and its error in under 2 minutes, without reading raw application logs." §2.1 traces it to the problem statement row: "'we don't know which step broke' | Requirement | R1, R2". R2 adds a measurable taxonomy target ("an 'unclassified' bucket that is itself alerted on and must trend to under 5% of failures") and NFR3 a measurable attribution time ("Median time from 'a failure alert fires' to 'we know which step and which category' ≤ 5 minutes").

expectations.text: The user's proposed technologies appear in the design or the tradeoff analysis, each tied to the requirement it would serve
expectations.evidence: §2.1's table gives every item a "The requirement it actually implies" cell and a "Where it is evaluated" cell: saga → R3 ("*If* checkout spans multiple systems that cannot share one transaction, then no attempt may leave money and order state inconsistent → R3"), microservices → "None identified from the stated problem. Decomposition is a means to team autonomy / independent scaling / independent deploys - none of which were stated as constraints", Redis → "None. Caching addresses latency or load; the stated problem is correctness/diagnosability", gRPC → "None. It presupposes the microservices split", flags → NFR2. Each then gets a full pros/cons/risk row: saga at §4.2 B2, microservices at §4.2 B3 and §4.4 D3, Redis at §4.4 D1, gRPC at §4.4 D2, flag platform at §4.3 C-ii. §4.4 is headed "proposals with no traceable requirement" and each row names what would give it one (e.g. D1 returns "If the measurement phase shows that the failure profile *is* dominated by dependency timeouts").

expectations.text: At least one of the user's proposed technologies is questioned, deferred, or shown not to be needed for the stated problem
expectations.evidence: §4.2: "B3 traces to no requirement in §2 and is therefore rejected *as a solution to this problem*." §4.4 D1 on Redis: "The premise is untested: no latency data, no timeout breakdown, no load ceiling, and no NFR in §2 that caching serves." §5.1: "Defer, do not reject: microservices (B3), gRPC (D2), Redis (D1)", and "Reversibility via C-i. Minimal runtime kill switches... Not a feature-flag platform - that is a separate decision needing an org-level driver and owner."

expectations.text: Where information is missing, the document either labels an assumption or asks a focused question with a recommended answer
expectations.evidence: §8 tabulates A-1 to A-11 with a "Changes the design if wrong?" column, and the labels are used inline where the gap bites (A-1 on the 2%, A-7 on placeholder step names, A-8 on single-process/single-DB as "most consequential"). §9 lists ten focused questions, the first three flagged as decision-changing, and §5.2 attaches the consequence of each answer ("Checkout already spans multiple services with separate databases (A-8 false) → B2 becomes mandatory immediately"). The reply names the single question it most wants answered and states its own default: "My design assumes the simpler case." The assertion's first branch (labelled assumptions) is amply met.

expectations.text: Every requirement in the document carries a goal and a stated way to prove it is met
expectations.evidence: No requirement carries a goal. The document has no goals section and no goal field or clause on any of R1-R5 or NFR1-NFR5; §3.4's traceability maps requirements to components, not to outcomes. Proof is also missing on several: R5 states only "Minimum 30 days queryable (assumption A-3; longer if a finance or compliance retention rule applies)" with no stated way to prove it; NFR2 states only "Every change introduced by this work is reversible in under 5 minutes without a code deploy" with no drill or measurement (and open question 7 concedes the current revert time is unknown); NFR4 states "No full card numbers, CVV, or track data in traces, logs, or the step ledger; PII minimized to identifiers" with no verification named in §2 (a schema review appears later, as a phase-2 gate); NFR5 explicitly has neither target nor proof - "No target number is given here because the current traffic volume is unknown (A-6)". The hypothesis table H1-H6 asks of each cause "Would a Rust/Go rewrite fix it?" and concludes "Only H5 makes a rewrite the *right* fix. expectations.text: Notes that the 12-second figure has not been attributed to a root cause, and names what would attribute it (a profile, a benchmark, or a breakdown by stage)

expectations.text: The tradeoff analysis includes at least one alternative that is not a rewrite in Rust or Go

expectations.text: Both alternatives the user named are still analysed fairly, with pros, cons and risks
expectations.evidence: "[Runtime] R3 - Rewrite in Go" carries pros (compiled, goroutines, static binary, short ramp, mature headless-Chromium drivers), cons (rewrite cost, parity risk, thinner document-layout ecosystem) and three risk rows. "[Runtime] R4 - Rewrite in Rust" carries pros (highest performance ceiling, no GC pauses, memory safety, Typst embeddable natively), cons (steepest ramp, slow compiles, smallest hiring pool) and four risk rows. expectations.text: Each functional requirement's proof is a concrete scenario (a role, a situation, an action, an observable result), not a restatement of the requirement

F1: 'Given an analyst signed in on an office laptop with an HTML file and its images, when they publish it to a chosen path, then the page is readable at that path on the company domain and no other person acted'. F2: 'Given a page published by someone else who is on holiday, when a colleague in the publisher group replaces its content, then the new version is live and the original author was not involved'. F3: 'Given a page replaced three times and then deleted, when a publisher asks for the version published before the last replacement, then that exact content is live again at its original path'.
